title: Promise.all, race, any, and allSettled
hook: Promise.all waits for every sibling and fails fast on the first rejection. Promise.allSettled never rejects — you inspect each outcome. Senior interviews pair these with production patterns: fan-out to microservices, partial failure handling, and racing fetch against a timeout.

blocks.text: **Promise.all(iterable)** returns a single Promise that fulfills with an array of results when all input Promises fulfill — or rejects immediately when any input rejects (fail-fast). **Promise.allSettled** waits for all to finish regardless of outcome, returning `{ status, value|reason }` objects. **Promise.race** fulfills or rejects with the first settled Promise. **Promise.any** fulfills with the first fulfillment — rejects only if all reject (AggregateError). These are static methods — they do not parallelize CPU; they overlap I/O waits on the single JS thread.

entries.plainDefinition: Concurrent wait for all fulfillments; first rejection rejects the combined Promise.
Wait for every input to settle; never rejects the wrapper Promise.
Adopt the state of the first Promise to settle — fulfillment or rejection.
Promise.all rejects as soon as one sibling rejects — others keep running but result is lost.
entries.example: One 404 in parallel batch rejects entire all().

blocks.text: Dashboard pages that fetch user profile, permissions, and notifications in parallel use Promise.all for latency — sequential await triples round-trip time. Batch jobs that must report per-item failures use allSettled. Timeout wrappers race fetch against a timer Promise. Misusing Promise.all when partial success is acceptable loses data on first failure. C# **Task.WhenAll** behaves like all; **Task.WhenAny** like race for completion.

blocks.title: Empty iterable edge case
blocks.body: Promise.all([]) fulfills immediately with []. Promise.any([]) rejects with AggregateError. Interviewers sometimes test this.

blocks.title: Sequential map instead of parallel
blocks.body: for (const url of urls) await fetch(url) is sequential. Use Promise.all(urls.map(u => fetch(u))) for overlap.

blocks.title: Race without aborting loser
blocks.body: Promise.race does not cancel the slower fetch — pass AbortSignal and abort when winner settles.

blocks.text: Implement Promise.all as interview follow-up after scratch Promise. Production: combine all with concurrency limit (module async-concurrency-limits) when URLs count in thousands — unbounded all opens thousands of sockets. Promise.any for redundant CDN endpoints — first success wins. TypeScript: `Promise.all([p1, p2] as const)` preserves tuple types.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying Promise.all runs on multiple threads. Confusing race and any. Not knowing all rejects on first failure. Cannot map to Task.WhenAll.

interviewTakeaways: Promise.all: parallel wait, fail-fast on first rejection, ordered results.
allSettled: never rejects wrapper — inspect status per item.
race: first settle wins; any: first fulfillment wins.
60s: all equals WhenAll — overlap I/O not CPU. allSettled for partial failure. race for timeout — abort loser. any for redundant endpoints. Empty all fulfills, empty any rejects.
Follow-up: implement Promise.all or add concurrency limit.
commonPitfalls: Weak: sequential await in loop calling it parallel.
Weak: race without AbortSignal — zombie requests continue.
Strong: 'all fail-fast. allSettled for degraded mode. Map to WhenAll. Bounded pool for thousands of tasks.'
